extracted.intended_audience: university mathematics faculty, curriculum designers, and administrators developing quantitative literacy/quantitative reasoning courses
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and assessing an interdisciplinary, technology‑infused undergraduate Quantitative Reasoning / Quantitative Literacy course for non‑majors, including learning goals, pedagogy, curriculum, assessment, and logistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core learning outcomes (summary list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Designed to enable students who have completed it to: Make and analyze quantitative arguments expressed in numerical, graphical, verbal, or symbolic forms; Interpret and create graphs summarizing quantitative data; Understand and use reasoning involving percentage change and proportional relationships; Make reasoned estimations; Use computer tools to analyze data; Make simple mathematical models (especially linear and exponential) and understand the limitations of mathematical models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit bulleted list defines the primary student competencies. Use these as target learning goals for course design, assignments, and assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite and placement policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The course has college algebra as a prerequisite; students can test out of college algebra via a placement exam. Students may also test out of the Quantitative Reasoning requirement via a specific examination or by placement into Calculus. Students in majors that require calculus are often exempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat prerequisite enforcement, test‑out options, and exemptions as program design choices tied to intended student population and curricular overlap with majors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence, criticality, and capability as program goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpose is to help students become confident, critical, and capable users of quantitative information (verbal, tabular, graphical, symbolic). Confidence is built through positive experiences; criticality through estimation exercises and critique of media graphics/articles; capability through skills with rates, percentages, graphs, models, correlations, and descriptive statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design assignments (e.g., math autobiography, media critiques) and assessments to explicitly measure these affective and cognitive goals, not just procedural skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology integration and in‑context tool use
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology (primarily Excel) is used throughout the course as a tool so students learn to use tools to solve real problems and produce realistic products. Approximately two‑thirds of class time is held in a computer lab with collaborative computer activities. Materials are delivered over the Internet; student products are Word documents or PowerPoint presentations with graphs pasted in from Excel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic datasets, frequent hands‑on activities, instructor facilitation during lab work, and require students to produce authentic deliverables to ensure tool mastery and transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of real, interdisciplinary data to increase engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every activity and every assignment has data with a social or scientific context; instructors bring data and examples from numerous fields to create wide appeal (e.g., ecology, political science, archaeology, economics, consumer statistics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select topical, socially relevant datasets (including those tied to campus programs like summer reading) to foster interdisciplinary connections and student interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active, collaborative, computer‑activity pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary pedagogy focuses on collaborative computer activities with instructor assistance; small class sizes (cap ~25) and a computer classroom with staff support are used to create an active, engaging learning environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize teamwork on lab tasks, scaffolded activities, and frequent formative feedback; be aware of and plan for group dynamics issues (see group‑work rubric below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimation skill standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimation is a critical skill. Specific guidelines: an estimate should start with basic, commonly accepted facts (population figures or basic quantities such as lengths, volumes); include the reasoning process by which the estimate is obtained; be expressed to an appropriate degree of precision (generally not too many decimal places).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess estimation by requiring students to show reasoning steps and to justify precision. Example tasks: estimate driving time across the US, annual mail delivered in US, heartbeats per day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentage reasoning mastery (five problem types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are asked to master five types of percentage problems that arise in everyday quantitative work: percentage as part of a whole, percent change, 'percent more than' problems, successive percent change problems, and reverse percentage change problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include diagnostics and targeted practice for each type; assessment data show these are commonly weak areas and require explicit instruction and repeated practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph creation, interpretation, and critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Students learn how to make and interpret pie charts, bar charts (including multiple bar charts), and XY‑graphs, when each type is appropriate, how to describe and interpret each type, and how to critique misleading graphs from the media. Introduce vocabulary for XY graphs (increasing, decreasing, constant, absolute/relative maxima and minima, periodicity, increasing/decreasing rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach graph choice heuristics, labeling and scaling best practices, and provide examples of media misuse for critique exercises; assess both production and interpretation skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical modeling standard (linear and exponential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach concept of mathematical modeling; review linear functions and linear models, use Excel to add simple regression lines, obtain equations and predictions, introduce R‑squared as a measure of goodness of fit; teach exponential modeling for contexts like population growth, investments, radioactive decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize model limitations: caution about extrapolation (less confidence the farther from data), interpretation of R‑squared, and matching model choice to context. Require students to produce at least one model with a prediction in major projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive statistics and correlation interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach basic descriptive statistics and how to determine if two variables are correlated using Excel. Heavy emphasis on interpretation of results, especially the possibility of common underlying causes for a correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess students on ability to compute summary statistics and correlation coefficients and to discuss plausible causal/confounding explanations rather than assuming causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final analytical project and presentation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Students produce an analytical paper (typically 8–10 pages including graphs) and a PowerPoint presentation. They must use at least three different tables (e.g., Statistical Abstract of the US) and make at least one mathematical model with a prediction. Projects are usually collaborative and all students must participate in the presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the project to synthesize skills: dataset selection, graphing, modeling, interpretation, and public‑policy recommendations. Grade both the written product and the presentation; address inequitable group contributions (see group‑work guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment strategy and diagnostics
rubrics_metrics.description: Program performs an annual assessment project that assesses one or more learning goals and includes direct examination of student work. Use of diagnostic exams, midterms, and finals to track gains (e.g., percentage problem subtypes showed measurable improvement across assessments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both direct (student work) and indirect (surveys) measures; track specific item performance to identify persistent weaknesses and guide curricular revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group work management and mitigation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Group‑based activities generally improve learning but present logistical and personal challenges (unequal participation, complacency in weaker students). Mitigations include requiring weekly individual out‑of‑class homework and structuring collaborative reports/presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design accountability measures (individual assignments, peer evaluation, documented contribution logs) to reduce free‑riding and ensure fair assessment of individual learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course length and reinforcement recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: A ten‑week (one‑quarter) course is probably not enough time; a semester or two quarters would be preferable, with further reinforcement through 'math across the curriculum' programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider extending course duration or adding curricular touchpoints across majors to improve transfer and mastery, especially for complex, free‑form final projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom and administrative supports
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional supports are critical: funding for a computer classroom, staff and student support, capped class sizes, and a program director to oversee curriculum, labs, and faculty development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for infrastructure, staffing, and faculty development when scaling the program; these supports correlate with program uniformity and success across many instructors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of media artifacts and critique as instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use articles and graphics from the media to analyze and critique quantitative arguments; finding errors or deception in published work builds criticality and student empowerment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate frequent media critique assignments, including reverse calculations and error‑finding exercises (example: identify numeric error in a Nature paragraph), to develop skeptical reading and verification habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curricular uniformity across diverse instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite many instructors (including from non‑math departments), it is important to maintain surprising uniformity across sections in content and approach; divergence from main outline and pedagogy should be rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide shared materials, a common course website, instructor training, and program oversight to ensure consistent learning experiences across instructors and sections.
